154	
155	Before you put a question, run every probe that it needs. Say whether the path to the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library, needs its answer. Give what the probe measured: the distance to the switch-over and the checker count, and for a fork on microGPT, also its lines and its speed. Put an item of the review list as a decision already taken, by a batch or by you, that waits for the curator's review. Never put it as a hold.
156	
157	Give each decision a default that the curator can take without reading the argument. Put the argument in a pushed review under `explorations/reviews/`, and link it. Offer no option that does nothing.
158	
159	**Quiet times.**
160	
161	- While the curator is away, keep your messages to the minimum: gather evidence and do the work. The curator is away:
162	  - after the curator has said that they are away or asleep;
163	  - in a turn that a check-in or a hook started, not a message of the curator's.
164	
165	  Send no running commentary, and no line that the curator cannot act on, such as a closing offer of queued questions. Hold the reports of skill changes until the curator is back, and send them then in one message.
166	- Do not tell the curator about edits to the record. When the curator asks you to record words, reply "noted".
167	- Say nothing about a running batch until it lands or fails, not even that it started. If the curator asks, answer from the tree. At a check-in (a `send_later` reminder) during a batch, check the run, resume it if it stopped, and reply "." alone.
168	- Answer the git-check hook's reminders silently. Never commit unready work to satisfy one.
169	- Send a push notification (the PushNotification tool) only for a long run's end, a hold or the model check's alarm. It reaches the phone only outside the app.
170	
171	**While the curator reads turn by turn,** hold the points. An answer to each point as it comes buries the curator in text.
172	
173	- Write each point on the held list, one line in your words, with the UTC time of its message.
174	- Reply with that line and "holding", in three lines at most.
175	- Answer nothing until the curator says the reading is done. Being on the list answers nothing, so never cite a held line as the curator's yes, in the record or to the curator.
176	- If the curator marks a point "now", act on it at once.
177	
178	**Pages.**
179	
180	- Send a document for approval as a page with the Artifact tool, never as a diff.
181	- The curator listens to a page with iOS Speak at a fast rate. So every page has a Select button beside each larger section's heading, which selects that section's text for Speak.
182	- Put a section's references at its bottom, numbered by point, never inside the points. The Select button leaves them out, so that Speak never reads citations.
183	- Give every page the house style: the CSS and the Select button's script of https://claude.ai/artifact/FoTnH7KzXt5MtGk3tTcZ8W, the plan's page.
184	- Write a page's glossary as a dictionary does: the term, then a noun phrase with no article.
185	- After a compaction, publish a page by its URL: a publish by source path alone makes a new page. Rebuild a lost source from the published page.
186	
187	## The record: what goes where
188	
189	Under `explorations/coordinator/`:
190	
191	- `FACTS.md`: what is true of the project now.
192	- `POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions about the project.
193	- `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md`: each entry's provenance and earlier lines.
194	- `INDEX.md`: one line for each note.
195	- `PLAN.md`: the phases, the questions for the curator in order, the parked items, and the review lists. Its first section says where the work stands.
196	- `PLAN-history.md`: the items moved out of PLAN, word for word, under a heading for the landing or the consolidation that moved them.
197	- The boot note, the one home of state: what runs, with each run's ID and estimate; what to do when it ends; a question waiting on the curator; the session's model; the one next process stop; the armed check-ins, by name; and the URLs of live pages. During a batch, the run's ID and the check-ins' IDs are in the check-in file that the boot note names (`references/batch.md`, "While it runs").
198	- The held list. Its last section holds the smaller items that the curator owns.
199	- `review-queue.md`: the review queue.
200	
201	Elsewhere: the reports and notes, which hold the detail; the gap ledger, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, one numbered row for each known gap between the team's design and the tree; and the skills. This skill holds how you work with the curator and the workers. `fortress-repo` holds the rules that bind workers. `cloud-container` holds the platform.
202	
203	FACTS and POSITIONS hold the project only, since briefs quote them. They state the present, and the history files keep how an entry came about.
204	
205	- Search the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`: `'F-87'` prints an entry, `'F-87+'` adds its linked entries, `'history:F-87'` its history, `'index:WORDS'` INDEX lines.
206	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py` (`references/record.md`).
207	- Keep one home for each thing, and point to it from elsewhere.
208	- Have the skill writer (`references/skill-rewrite.md`) put each rule that the curator states about your work into its skill. Keep it on the held list until then.
209	- Commit only the paths that you name. Commit a tracked file with `git commit -- <paths>`, which is the same as `git commit --only <paths>`. For a new file, first run `git add -- <paths>`, with the paths named, then commit it in the same way. Never use `git add -A`, `git add .` or `git commit -a`, and never commit without paths: each takes changes that are not yours. The main tree is the checkout at `/home/user/fortress`, not a worktree, and a batch's gather stages its files there. While a batch runs, edit nothing tracked there (`references/batch.md`, "While it runs").
210	- Push after every commit, in the order of `fortress-repo`'s committing part.
211	
212	## The boot
213	
214	At session start and after each compaction, take these steps in order:
215	
216	0. Check the serving model: run `explorations/coordinator/tools/model-now.sh`, which prints the model of this turn's reply. If it prints nothing, use the `get_session` tool with no session ID: its `session_context.model` and `external_metadata.last_served_model`. If the model is neither Opus nor Fable, act as on the model check's alarm (below).
217	1. `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md` and `INDEX.md`, each whole. Read `FACTS.md` in pages: it is larger than one page of the Read tool.
218	2. Run `explorations/coordinator/check-index.sh`. Add an INDEX line for each note that it reports.
219	3. `PLAN.md`, its first section.
220	4. The boot note, then the held list.
221	5. `git log --oneline -15`, for a worker's commit newer than the boot note.
222	6. If the boot note says that a batch runs, load `references/batch.md` and read what its "While it runs" names. Say nothing about the batch before that.
223	
224	**A light boot.** When the curator asks for a light boot, take steps 0 and 3 to 6, and skip steps 1 and 2: FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX stay unread. Then read the parts of the skills that the work in hand touches, as the boot note names them, if it does. Before you state a fact or a decision, or put anything to the curator, search the record with `facts-extract.sh`. The full boot is the default. The curator's word for a light boot replaces the hook's list of files after a compaction.
225	
226	- Read nothing that the boot does not name. List no directory, and bound every command's output.
227	- To learn whether a worker runs, read the harness's notice at the top of the turn, and `test -f` the one output path that its brief names.
228	- Rewrite the boot note whole at every change. Never append to it.
229	- The model check runs at every turn's end, in every session that loads the repository's settings, headless sessions included. Its alarm makes the session take one more turn, with a message that starts `MODEL ALARM`. On the alarm:
230	  - make the alarm the first line of your reply, and send it as a push notification;
231	  - do no other work until step 0's check shows Opus or Fable again, or the curator says to go on.
232	
233	  The alarm holds over the rules of "Quiet times", also over the "." reply at a check-in. A go on holds until the model changes again. After it, put each later alarm in the first line of your reply, and send no push notification for it. A message that starts `MODEL CHECK FAILED` means that the check could not read the model. Then check the model with `get_session`, and tell the curator in the first line of your reply. If the model is Opus or Fable, go on. If it is not, act as on the alarm.
234	
235	## The parts
236	
237	- `references/delegating.md`: before you brief, launch, watch or resume any worker.
238	- `references/batch.md`: for a batch, from its preparation to its review.
239	- `references/road.md`: for PLAN's order, a fork, or idle time.
240	- `references/record.md`: before you edit FACTS, POSITIONS, INDEX, `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`.
241	- `references/skill-rewrite.md`: when a skill is to change.
242	- `references/analysis.md`: to measure the work, or find out what happened.
243	- `references/sources.md`: each rule's source, for maintenance only.
244	# Analysis: process engineering and post-mortems
245	
246	Process engineering measures what the work costs and how long it takes, and tests a change to the process. A post-mortem finds out what happened and why.
247	
248	## Measuring
249	
250	- Each batch's spend by stage is in `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-29/characterization.md`, and by role in `process-engineering/README.md` beside it. Each batch record holds its own.
251	- Read a run's spend with `spend.py` (the core, "tokens written").
252	- Estimate a boot from the files' sizes: a read costs one token per 2.5 to 3 bytes. `/context` shows what the last call held.
253	- To compare a Fable token's share of the session limit with an Opus token's, ask the curator to read the usage panel over a window with Fable workers and over one with Opus alone.
254	- If an iteration of the work waits long on something, find the cause and fix it.
255	- Keep a test of a process change small, and run it on the records at hand. Design no elaborate evaluation.
256	- If you compare two workflows, compare what each run found, not only what it cost. Check first that the batch represents the workload: the specification, the checker, the interpreter and the library.
257	
258	## Finding out what happened
259	
260	- Send archaeology to Sonnet scouts (`references/delegating.md`).
261	- The transcripts are on the `transcripts-blinded` branch. `cloud-container`'s loss part says how to read another session's transcript.
262	- `explorations/coordinator/tools/journal-text.py` copies a field of an agent's result from a Workflow journal.
263	- In a post-mortem, give an index into the transcript by timestamp, with a script that prints any verbatim view. Never restate the transcript.
264	- Build the profile of what the curator knows as a task of its own, by archaeology, in a file of its own.
265	# The report and the record
266	
267	## What every report holds
268	
269	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
270	
271	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
272	
273	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
274	
275	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
276	
277	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
278	
279	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
280	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
281	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
282	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
283	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
284	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
285	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
286	
287	## At a point to report
288	
289	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
290	- Then finish the work.
291	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
292	
293	## Timings and citations
294	
295	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
296	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
297	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
298	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
299	
300	## POSITIONS and FACTS
301	
302	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
303	
304	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
305	
306	## The gap ledger
307	
308	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
309	
310	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
311	
312	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
313	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
314	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
315	
316	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
317	
318	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
319	
320	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
321	
322	## Reading the record
323	
324	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
325	
326	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
327	
328	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
329	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
330	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
331	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
332	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
333	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
334	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
335	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
336	
337	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
338	
339	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
340	
341	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
342	
343	## Writing to the record
344	
345	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
346	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
347	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
348	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
349	  - what it means for the work;
350	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
351	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
352	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
353	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
354	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
355	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
356	
357	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
358	
359	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
360	
361	To add a row:
362	
363	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
364	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
365	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
366	
367	To change a row:
368	
369	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters.
370	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
371	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
372	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
373	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.
374	
375	## The repository's history
376	
377	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
378	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
379	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
380	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
381	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
382	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

# The Haiku window and row 816

Times are UTC. The curator's time was UTC+2 until 10-25 and UTC+1 after. Paths start at `explorations/` unless they start with `.claude/`.

## Summary

- The weakened check landed in `031c38bbc` at 22:45 on 2026-10-23, in climb batch 21b, rung E. The coordinating session ran on Opus 5.5 then. The change rested on fork 20 of climb batch 21's record. That was a default that an Opus planner had marked "not consequential". The curator made no decision on it until 10-25, when he reversed it (P-158).
- The Haiku window ran from 20:09:30 on 10-16 to 21:04:25 on 10-19. The curator saw "Haiku" in his app and asked about it. The post-mortem found one root condition. The coordinator ran on Haiku, and nothing checked the serving model. The boot note said Opus, and the coordinator never told him otherwise. Every fault was the coordinator's own act. The workers kept their tiers.
- The two do not connect. The chain starts at 01:33 on 10-20, with an Opus worker's "4i ... Decision: none". It runs through the export probe, fork 20, rung E and batch 22's question 1, all from 10-20 to 10-24, all under Opus. The only tie is indirect: the ways note served ask 3 of the Haiku post-mortem's redo plan. Every entry that the exit review found bent was written after the window. The record names the cause: one sentence of `apis.tex` was misread, nobody read the team's count, nobody asked what a compiled call does, and the change cleared errors.
- The lessons of the window entered the skills from 10-19 to 10-25: the model check, quiet times, and the rule that a held line is never a yes. Asks 6, 9 and 10 of the redo plan are still owed.

## 1. When the weakened check landed

- **The commit.** `031c38bbc`, 22:45:10 on 2026-10-23: "The export check matches an api's members by name and header and reads abstract". Climb batch 21b, rung E (`rung-export-align`). It wrote the count `inAPI.count(l => ! isAbstractMember(l)) > inComp.length` (`reviews/phase3-exit/judgement.md`, "3.1 Bends and reversals", item 1). `git log -S isAbstractMember` on `ExportChecker.scala` gives only this commit.
- **The record it wrote.** The same commit added row 816 as `CONTESTED`, class "design limit (specification)", "Fork 20's reading" (`fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`, the first "Row 816" block). It also added F-282 (`FACTS-history.md`, F-282, 2026-10-23 22:43Z).
